bekhorot-3b-10-10.note: Rav Mari bar Rahel had a flock of animals. He would transfer ownership of the ears of the unborn firstborn to a gentile, which removed their firstborn status, yet he still forbade shearing them or working them and gave them to the priests, as if they were ordinary firstborns. In the end, the animals of Rav Mari bar Rahel died.
bekhorot-3b-10-10.why: The Gemara has just told of Rava ruling that no one follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that an animal partly owned by a gentile still has firstborn status; Rav Mari's case uses that exemption, and the Gemara then asks why his animals died.

people.name: Rav Mari bar Rahel
people.about: A Sage who sold the ears of his firstborn animals to a gentile, and whose animals died

terms.meaning: The first male born to a kosher cow, sheep or goat is holy by Torah law: it may not be sheared or worked, and is given to a priest.
Selling even a small part of an unborn animal to a gentile makes it jointly owned, which exempts it from firstborn status.
A non-Jew.

bekhorot-5a-7-11.note: Kontrokos, a government officer, put two questions to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai. First: the Levite families add up to 22,300, yet the tribe's total is given as 22,000, so where did 300 go? Rabban Yohanan answered that those 300 were themselves firstborns, and a firstborn cannot redeem another firstborn. Then: Moses collected 201 talents and 11 maneh of silver, but the text records giving only 100 talents. Was Moses a thief, a gambler, or bad at arithmetic? Rabban Yohanan answered that Moses was a trustworthy treasurer and expert in accounts, but the Sanctuary's maneh was double the ordinary one.
bekhorot-5a-7-11.why: The Gemara has been discussing the firstborn in the wilderness and how the Levites took their place; this exchange explains why 300 Levites could not count toward that exchange, and the Gemara then examines where the doubled maneh comes from.

people.name: Kontrokos
people.about: A government officer who challenges the Torah's numbers

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who answers both of Kontrokos's challenges

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who explains why a firstborn Levite cannot redeem an Israelite firstborn

people.name: Moses
people.about: Leader who collected and gave the Tabernacle silver; Kontrokos accuses him and Rabban Yohanan defends him

terms.meaning: Members of the tribe of Levi, who took the place of the Israelite firstborn in sacred service; each Levite redeemed one firstborn.
Units of silver weight. Here a talent is 60 maneh, and an ordinary maneh is 25 shekels.
The portable sanctuary the Israelites built in the wilderness, funded partly by a half-shekel from every man.

bekhorot-6b-3-4.note: Shimon HaAmasoni used to draw a new teaching from every occurrence of the small Hebrew word "et" in the Torah. When he reached "You shall fear the Lord your God," which also has "et," he gave the method up, since nothing could be added to the fear of God. His students asked what would become of all the "et"s he had already interpreted. He answered that just as he was rewarded for interpreting them, he would be rewarded for withdrawing. The verse stayed unexplained until Rabbi Akiva came and taught that its "et" includes Torah scholars, who must also be feared.
bekhorot-6b-3-4.why: The Gemara has just said that Rabbi Shimon derives the ban on camel's milk from the word "et," while the Rabbis do not interpret "et" at all; this teaching is cited to show where the Rabbis' refusal comes from.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: A Sage who interpreted every "et" in the Torah, then withdrew from the method

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who later explained the "et" in the verse about fearing God

terms.meaning: A small Hebrew word marking the object of a verb, with no meaning of its own in translation; some Sages read it as hinting at something extra.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

bekhorot-8b-3-20.note: The Roman emperor asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya how long a snake is pregnant. He said seven years; the emperor objected that the sages of Athens had bred snakes that gave birth in three. Rabbi Yehoshua said the Jews were wiser, and the emperor dared him to defeat the sixty Athenian sages and bring them back. Sailing to Athens, he tricked a butcher into showing him their hidden school, used reversed sandal prints to get its guards killed, and beat the sages at riddles: a house in the air, a field of knives, eggs of a black hen. Lodged in his ship, they were carried to the emperor. Soil from Athens restored their arrogance, the emperor let Rabbi Yehoshua do as he wished, and they were defeated by a jug that swallowed water until their shoulders gave out.
bekhorot-8b-3-20.why: The Gemara has been working out snakes' gestation from the curse on the snake in Genesis, reaching seven years; the story opens with that same figure, which Rabbi Yehoshua defends before the emperor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: The Jewish Sage who answers the emperor and outwits the sages of Athens

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman ruler who questions Rabbi Yehoshua and sends him to Athens

people.name: the sages of Athens
people.about: Sixty wise men in a guarded school whom Rabbi Yehoshua defeats in a contest of riddles

terms.meaning: A place in the sea where, the text says, the water swallows everything near it; water taken from there will not fill a vessel.
A sacred name of God which, in Talmudic stories, a Sage can say aloud to work wonders, as Rabbi Yehoshua does to float in the air.

bekhorot-27a-10-10.note: Rav Nahman, Rav Amram and Rami bar Hama were travelling on a ferry. While Rav Amram stepped away to relieve himself, a woman came and asked the other two whether someone made impure by a corpse may immerse in a ritual bath and then eat teruma grown outside the Land of Israel. Rav Nahman said to Rami bar Hama: do we even have the sprinkling of the red heifer's ashes? Rami bar Hama suggested they wait for the old man, Rav Amram. Meanwhile Rav Amram returned and said that Rav taught: such a person may immerse and eat teruma from outside the Land.
bekhorot-27a-10-10.why: Shmuel has just ruled that teruma from outside the Land of Israel is forbidden only to someone whose impurity comes from his own body, not to one who touched a corpse; the ferry question tests that, and the Gemara afterward rules that the law does not follow Rav Amram's report.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: One of three Sages on the ferry; he doubts that immersion can help without the red heifer

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: The older Sage of the three, who returns and reports Rav's ruling

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: Sage on the ferry who suggests waiting for Rav Amram

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage whose ruling Rav Amram quotes

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which must be eaten only in a state of ritual purity.

terms.term: impure through contact with a corpse
terms.meaning: The most severe kind of ritual impurity, which by Torah law is removed only by sprinkling with water mixed with the ashes of a red heifer.

terms.term: sprinkling of the ashes of the red heifer
terms.meaning: The purification rite for corpse impurity, which could no longer be performed in the Sages' time.
A pool of natural water (mikveh) in which a person immerses to become ritually pure.

bekhorot-29b-14-14.note: A butcher was suspected of selling the forbidden fat near the kidney as permitted intestinal fat. Rava penalized him by forbidding him to sell even nuts. Rav Pappa asked whether Rava was following the stricter view, in which case he should forbid even water and salt. Rava explained that the penalty was tied to the offense itself: the butcher had used nuts, which children love, to lure butchers' children into bringing him the forbidden fat, which he then sold as permitted.
bekhorot-29b-14-14.why: The mishna has just set out a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one may buy nothing at all from a suspect seller, and Rabbi Shimon says only items connected to his offense are barred. Rava shows his ruling fits Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who penalizes the butcher.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who questions which opinion Rava's penalty follows.

terms.meaning: Certain fats of cattle, sheep and goats, such as the fat around the kidneys, that the Torah forbids to be eaten, while other fat is permitted.

bekhorot-30b-12-14.note: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei were unsure about a question of ritual purity, and the Sages sent students to ask the son of Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus to look into it. They found him carrying ritually pure items; he seated Sages from his own school beside the students, not trusting the students with his pure items, and stood to examine the question. The students reported this to Rabbi Yehuda, who said angrily that this man's father degraded Torah scholars and the son does too. Rabbi Yosei answered: let the elder's honor stay in its place. Since the Temple was destroyed, priests have held themselves to a higher standard and do not hand pure items to anyone.
bekhorot-30b-12-14.why: A teaching has just required even a Torah scholar to commit, before three members, to the purity rules of a haver; Rabbi Yohanan dates that rule to this incident, when scholars were not trusted with pure items.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Sage who says when the ruling about Torah scholars was taught

people.name: the son of Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus
people.about: A priest who does not trust the visiting students with his ritually pure items

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage who is unsure of the purity question and is angered by the treatment of the students

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who defends the priest's conduct

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus
people.about: The priest's father, whom Rabbi Yehuda accuses of degrading Torah scholars

terms.meaning: Food or objects kept in a state of ritual purity, which can be made impure by contact with someone who is not careful about purity rules.
Literally 'associate': a person who has formally committed to keep strict rules of ritual purity and tithing.

bekhorot-30b-17-17.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reported in the name of Rabbi Meir an incident about a woman who was married to a haver and would tie his phylacteries on his hand. Later she married a tax collector, and she would tie tax seals on his hand.
bekhorot-30b-17-17.why: The Sages are debating whether the household of a haver who move into the home of someone less observant must formally take on the haver's commitments again; Rabbi Meir says they must, and the incident shows how fully a wife's practice follows her husband.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who holds that even these people must take on the commitments, and in whose name the incident is told.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident.

terms.meaning: A member of a fellowship devoted to careful observance, especially of ritual purity and tithes.
Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah verses, bound on the arm and head during prayer.
Marks or tokens a tax collector wore, here bound on the hand where phylacteries had been.

bekhorot-31a-4-5.note: The Sages once needed Rav Huna bar Hiyya for some matter, and Rabba, Rav Yosef and four hundred pairs of Sages went up to his home; hearing they were coming, he set out four hundred chairs for them. Later they heard he had become a tax collector and sent word: go to your important post, and to your former status. He replied that he had repented and was no longer a tax collector. Rav Yosef did not go to him, but Rabba did. Rav Yosef cited a teaching that one who leaves tax collecting is not accepted back; Rabba cited its later version, that such a man is like anyone else.
bekhorot-31a-4-5.why: A teaching has just recorded that the Sages first barred a haver who became a tax collector even after he quit, and later changed their minds; Rav Yosef and Rabba each act on one stage of that teaching.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: A man the Sages needed, who became a tax collector and later said he had repented

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Sage who goes to Rav Huna bar Hiyya after he repents

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who refuses to go, holding that a former tax collector is not taken back

terms.meaning: In the Sages' world, a tax collector was seen as untrustworthy, so a haver who took the job lost his standing.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

bekhorot-31b-7-8.note: Rav Sheshet was troubled by a problem one night and solved it in the morning from a baraita. His attendant, Rav Idi, heard the solution from him and repeated it in the study hall without saying it was Rav Sheshet's. When Rav Sheshet heard, he was annoyed and said: the one who stung me, let him be stung by a scorpion.
bekhorot-31b-7-8.why: The Gemara has found a contradiction over whether the meat of an animal tithe may be sold, which Rav Sheshet resolved. It explains his anger with Rav's teaching that David prayed for his words to be quoted in his name: a scholar quoted by name moves his lips in the grave.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage who solves a legal problem overnight and is angered when his answer is repeated without his name.

people.name: Rav Idi
people.about: Rav Sheshet's attendant, who repeats the solution in the study hall without crediting him.

people.name: David
people.about: King David, who according to Rav asked God that people repeat his teachings in his name after his death.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
Every tenth newborn animal of the herd, which is consecrated; its meat may normally not be sold.
The place where the Sages and their students gathered to learn and debate.

bekhorot-36a-8-9.note: A man rented his donkey to another and told him not to take the path of Nehar Pekod, where there was water, but the dry path of Neresh. The renter took the Nehar Pekod path anyway and the donkey died. When he came back he admitted going that way but claimed there had been no water. Rava said his claim is believed, since if he wanted to lie he could have said he took the Neresh path; Abaye answered that this 'why would he lie' reasoning is not used where witnesses can settle the matter.
bekhorot-36a-8-9.why: Rabbi Ile'a has ruled that a priest is believed when he says a blemish on his firstborn animal happened by accident. Mar bar Rav Ashi raises the donkey case to challenge this; the Gemara answers that there the water was certain, while here the priest's tampering is only a suspicion.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who raises this earlier case as an objection to the ruling under discussion.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rules that the renter is believed, since he could have told an easier lie.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Disputes Rava: the 'why would he lie' argument does not apply where witnesses are available.

terms.meaning: A rule of evidence: if a person could have won with a simpler, more convenient claim but made a less convenient one instead, his claim is believed, since a liar would have chosen the easier story.

bekhorot-36a-11-15.note: Rabbi Tzadok, a priest, had a firstborn animal whose lip split while it ate barley from a wicker basket. He asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether a learned priest is treated differently from an ignorant one in such a case, and was told yes. Rabban Gamliel told him no, and when the scholars gathered in the study hall the question was asked publicly. Rabbi Yehoshua now said no; Rabban Gamliel ordered him to stand while witnesses testified against him, and Rabbi Yehoshua admitted that the living cannot contradict the living. Rabban Gamliel went on lecturing while Rabbi Yehoshua stood, until the crowd murmured and told Hutzpit, the one relaying the lecture, to stop, and he stopped.
bekhorot-36a-11-15.why: The discussion is about whether a priest is believed that a blemish on his own firstborn animal was not caused on purpose. Rabbi Tzadok's question, whether a learned priest is trusted more than an ignorant one, is exactly that issue, and the mishna that follows continues it.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: A learned priest whose firstborn animal was blemished; he brings the question to both Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tells Rabbi Tzadok privately that a learned priest is treated differently, then says otherwise in public.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The Nasi, head of the academy; he rules otherwise and makes Rabbi Yehoshua stand during his lecture.

people.name: Hutzpit
people.about: The disseminator who repeated Rabban Gamliel's lecture aloud to the crowd; the people tell him to stop.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat belongs to a priest and is holy. It may be eaten as ordinary meat only if it has a permanent blemish, so priests were suspected of causing blemishes on purpose.
A learned and careful person, trusted to keep the laws; the opposite of an ignoramus.
The president of the Sages' council and head of the academy.
A speaker who repeated a Sage's lecture in a loud voice so the whole assembly could hear it.

bekhorot-36b-6-6.note: Rafram, in Pumbedita, gave his firstborn animal to a priest unblemished, and the priest went and caused a blemish in it. One day, when Rafram's eyes were afflicted, the priest brought the animal before him to be declared fit, saying an Israelite had given it to him already blemished. Rafram forced his eyes open, recognized the animal, and said to him: Is it not I who gave this to you?
bekhorot-36b-6-6.why: Rav ruled that a priest is believed when he says an Israelite gave him a firstborn already blemished, and Pumbedita taught it that way. The Gemara adds that Rafram still kept trusting other priests: only this one was so brazen.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: A Sage in Pumbedita who examined firstborn animals; he had given this animal to the priest himself.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat is given to a priest and is holy. He may eat it as ordinary meat only once an expert confirms a permanent blemish, so priests were suspected of causing blemishes.

bekhorot-38b-4-5.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar recalled an elder in his neighborhood, Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya, whom he had never passed in front of. Once he did, and the elder said: Sit, my son, sit. He taught him that the 'snail' growth in a firstborn's eye is a permanent blemish, allowing the animal to be slaughtered, and that it is the same as the 'snake' the Sages mention. He added that although a person may not judge blemishes for himself, a teacher may teach his students the law and the students may then rule for him.
bekhorot-38b-4-5.why: The mishna lists a 'snail' and a 'snake' among eye blemishes, and the Sages asked whether these are one blemish or two. This account answers that they are the same. The Gemara then asks how a ruling made for the elder's own benefit could be trusted.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: Passes on the account he heard from Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar
people.about: The narrator, who once passed before the elder and was taught by him.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya
people.about: An elder in Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar's neighborhood who teaches him about the eye blemish.

terms.meaning: A lasting physical defect that disqualifies a firstborn animal from the altar, so it may be slaughtered and eaten as ordinary meat.
The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat, which is holy and belongs to a priest.

bekhorot-40a-7-7.note: In Piran of Beit Menahem, a firstborn animal seemed to have only one testicle. Someone mashed its sac to see whether a second one would come out, and none did. The animal was slaughtered, and the testicle was found attached to the loins. Rabbi Akiva permitted the meat, and Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri prohibited it.
bekhorot-40a-7-7.why: The mishna lists a missing testicle as a blemish and gives Rabbi Akiva's test: mash the sac and see if one emerges. This teaching adds the place of the incident; the two Sages' sharp exchange over it follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Reports the incident in a baraita.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Permitted the animal's meat, since the testicle had not emerged when tested.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: Prohibited the animal's meat.

terms.meaning: The firstborn male of a cow, sheep or goat is holy and may be eaten as ordinary meat only if it has a blemish; without one it is a sacrifice.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.

bekhorot-44a-17-17.note: A teaching listed the tzime'ah among the blemishes that keep a priest from serving in the Temple, but the Sages did not know what the word meant. They heard an Arab calling out, 'Who wants a tzime'ah?', and it turned out to be a long-eared goat.
bekhorot-44a-17-17.why: The mishna lists ear blemishes, the tzomem and the tzome'a, that disqualify a priest, and a baraita adds the tzime'ah. The overheard Arab is how the Sages learned what that word means.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core law code the Gemara discusses.
An unusual word for a bodily blemish; from the Arab's use, the Sages learned it describes long ears, as on a long-eared goat.

bekhorot-44b-2-2.note: Shmuel needed to urinate on the Shabbat when crowds gathered to hear the laws of the coming Festival, and people spread a sheet around him for privacy. His father said he would give him four hundred dinars to go and undo the impression this had made. You can have a sheet held up, he said, but should someone who cannot endanger himself by holding back?
bekhorot-44b-2-2.why: Rabbi Abba has just taught that Torah scholars may urinate in public, since holding back harms the body, and a baraita tells of a man whose belly swelled from holding back. Shmuel's father wants that permission seen to apply to everyone, not only those who can arrange privacy.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who needed to relieve himself during a public gathering and was screened with a sheet.

people.name: his father
people.about: Shmuel's father, who offers him money to correct the example he set.

terms.meaning: One of the pilgrimage holidays (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot). On the Shabbat before one, crowds came to hear its laws taught.
A silver coin; four hundred was a very large sum.

bekhorot-44b-3-3.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi needed to urinate while crossing the beams of a bridge, and he did. People told him his mother-in-law was coming. He told them he would have done it even in her ear.
bekhorot-44b-3-3.why: The Gemara has ruled that one may urinate in public rather than hold back and endanger one's health; it follows Shmuel's story with this one, and goes on to explain the harm holding back can do.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who relieves himself on a bridge and is not deterred when told his mother-in-law is approaching.

bekhorot-45a-16-16.note: The students of Rabbi Yishmael boiled the body of a prostitute whom the king had sentenced to death by burning, to separate the flesh from the bones. They counted and found 252 limbs, more than the 248 the Sages taught. They were told, by Shmuel according to the English translation: Perhaps you examined a woman, for Scripture added to her two hinges and two doors.
bekhorot-45a-16-16.why: The discussion concerns how many bones make up a majority of a human body for the laws of corpse impurity, based on 248 limbs. The story shows a woman's body counted with four more, and the Gemara then uses it against Rabbi Akiva, who says she also has a 'key'.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: The Sage whose students carried out the examination.

terms.meaning: Here, a bone with flesh and sinew on it. The Sages counted 248 in the human body.
The Sages' figurative names, drawn from verses about childbirth, for parts of a woman's body involved in giving birth, which they counted as extra limbs.

bekhorot-45b-2-2.note: Rabbi Yehuda reported that a man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all, came before Rabbi Tarfon, who said to him: May those like you increase among the Jewish people! Rabbi Yosei objected that this proves nothing: what Rabbi Tarfon really said was, May the mamzerim and Gibeonites be like you, so that they decrease from the Jewish people.
bekhorot-45b-2-2.why: The mishna records a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says a priest with extra fingers and toes may serve, the Rabbis say he may not. Rabbi Yehuda brings Rabbi Tarfon's words as a sign that extra digits are no blemish; Rabbi Yosei turns the same words into an insult.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Tells the story as proof that extra fingers and toes are not a blemish.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The Sage before whom the man with twenty-four digits came.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Disputes Rabbi Yehuda's version of what Rabbi Tarfon said.

terms.meaning: Children of a forbidden union, such as adultery, who are restricted in whom they may marry.
Descendants of the Gibeonites who joined Israel in Joshua's time; they too were restricted from marrying into ordinary Jewish families.

bekhorot-50a-6-6.note: Rav Ashi sent seventeen dinars to Rav Aha, son of Ravina, a priest, to redeem a firstborn son, with a message: let the Master send back the extra third of a dinar included in the sum. Rav Aha sent back: let the Master send me the other three dinars the Sages added to the coin.
bekhorot-50a-6-6.why: The Gemara has just reconciled two values of the Torah's shekel by explaining that the Sages later raised its value by a sixth. The two letters show the gap: by the old value seventeen dinars was slightly too much, by the raised value it was three short.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sends money for redeeming a firstborn son and asks for change.

people.name: Rav Aha, son of Ravina
people.about: The priest who received the money and replied that more was owed.

terms.meaning: A father pays a priest five sela, Torah-era silver coins, to redeem his firstborn son, as the Torah commands.
A silver coin; the value of the Torah's sela was reckoned in dinars, and the Sages raised it.

bekhorot-50b-10-10.note: Hanan the wicked struck a man, and the man came before Rav Huna, who ordered Hanan to give him half a dinar. Hanan had only a worn dinar that was no longer in circulation. So he struck the man a second time and gave him the whole dinar.
bekhorot-50b-10-10.why: Rav Asi has just taught that sums fixed by the Sages are in cheaper provincial coin, so the one-sela fine for an insulting blow is only half a dinar. Rav Huna's ruling applies that small fine, which Hanan treats as a price.

people.name: Hanan the wicked
people.about: A man who struck another, and struck him again to use up a whole coin.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The judge who fined Hanan half a dinar.

terms.meaning: A silver coin. The fine for an insulting slap was a small 'sela' in local coin, worth half a dinar.

bekhorot-51b-5-5.note: Rabbi Hanina, a priest, used to take the money for redeeming a firstborn son and give it back. Once he saw that a father who had paid him kept walking back and forth in front of him, hinting that he wanted it returned. Rabbi Hanina said: you never fully meant to give it. That is a bad thing, and therefore his son is not redeemed.
bekhorot-51b-5-5.why: A baraita has just ruled that if the priest returns the redemption money the father has still fulfilled his duty, and Rabbi Tarfon did this regularly. This story shows the limit: the father must truly give the money.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A priest who would return the redemption money he received.

terms.meaning: A father pays a priest five silver coins to redeem his firstborn son, as the Torah commands.

bekhorot-57b-2-4.note: Rabbi Yishmael ben Satriel of Arkat Leveina testified before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that in his place, when a mother animal died, they flayed her and dressed the living newborn in her skin. Rabbi said this revealed the reason for the mishna's ruling. He also reported lettuce with 600,000 leaves in its core, a fallen cedar so wide sixteen wagons drove along it side by side, and a bar yokhani egg that fell, drowned sixty cities and broke three hundred cedars. The Gemara asks how that bird could drop an egg when it lays on the ground; Rav Ashi said the egg was unfertilized.
bekhorot-57b-2-4.why: The Gemara has just cited Rabbi Yehoshua: a newborn whose mother died is not an 'orphan' if her hide is there, which matters for tithing animals. The flaying custom explains why, since the hide stands in for the mother.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Satriel
people.about: A man from Arkat Leveina who reports the customs and wonders of his home before Rabbi.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, before whom the testimony is given; he says it explains the mishna.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Explains why the egg fell: it was unfertilized.

terms.meaning: Here, a newborn animal whose mother died. Such an animal is excluded from the animal tithe unless the mother's hide is present.
A legendary giant bird, which the Sages identified with a bird described in the book of Job.
